candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 35 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 36 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 37 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 38 not required. 39
candidates.context: 4 In this guidance, the terms drugs or drug product include human drugs and biological products unless otherwise specified.

candidates.statement: Protocol deviations are generally unintentional departures from the IRB-approved protocol and 44 are commonly not discovered until after they occur (e.g., an investigator’s failure to perform a 45 protocol-required test is discovered by the study monitor during a routine monitoring visit). 46 Protocol deviations may also include an intentional departure from the IRB-approved protocol 47 for a single participant (e.g., investigator seeks and receives sponsor and IRB approval to enroll a 48 participant above the maximum age criteria); such intentional departures should be rare because 49 the protocol should include appropriate flexibility regarding trial conduct (e.g., eligibility 50 criteria, reasonable visit windows). In the conduct of a clinical investigation, however, some 51 deviations from the specifics outlined in the protocol may occur. In 2013, FDA issued the 52 International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guidance for industry E3 Structure and Content 53 of Clinical Study Reports: Questions and Answers (R1) , which includes clarifications for 54 implementing the recommendations in the ICH guidance for industry E3 Structure and Content 55 of Clinical Study Reports (July 1996) regarding the structure and content of a clinical study 56 report. To help clarify recommendations regarding the reporting of protocol deviations as 57 recommended in ICH E3, ICH E3(R1) defines a protocol deviation as “any change, divergence, 58 or departure from the study design or procedures defined in the protocol” and defines important 59 protocol deviations as “a subset of protocol deviations that might significantly affect the 60
candidates.context: completeness, accuracy, and/or reliability of the study data or that might significantly affect a 61 subject’s rights, safety, or well-being.” 5 In this guidance, FDA is adopting the ICH E3(R1) 62 definitions of protocol deviation and important protocol deviation. 63

candidates.statement: Clinical studies are conducted in accordance with the protocol, good clinical practice (GCP) 76 guidelines, 6 and regulatory requirements governing the design, conduct, performance, 77 monitoring, auditing, recording, analysis, and reporting of clinical studies. 7 Although protocols 78 may directly reference GCP guidelines or requirements, FDA does not consider all potential 79 GCP compliance issues to be protocol deviations. For example, if a monitor discovers that the 80 site delegation log is missing a signature of one of the site study staff, this missing signature 81 should be addressed, but it is not considered a protocol deviation because the protocol likely does 82 not specify this level of detail at the site level. Classifying potential GCP compliance issues as 83 protocol deviations can inflate the number of events submitted to sponsors, FDA, and IRBs. 84 FDA recommends that potential GCP compliance issues that are not deviations from the protocol 85 be managed outside the protocol deviation process outlined in this guidance. 86

For the most recent version of a guidance, check the FDA guidance web page at https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents .

candidates.statement: Thoughtful protocol design can help to minimize important protocol deviations. In general, 124 deviations that are classified as important should be those that could affect critical-to-quality 125 factors 9 for the trial; protocol deviations related to critical-to-quality elements should be 126 identified. The quality by design approach to clinical research involves focusing on these 127 critical-to-quality factors to ensure the protection of the rights, safety, and well-being of study 128 participants; the generation of reliable and meaningful results; and the management of risks to 129 those factors using a risk-proportionate approach. 10 Examples of critical-to-quality factors are 130 procedures and processes that affect the protection of trial participants and/or the efficacy or 131 safety analyses (e.g., accuracy in certain eligibility criteria, accuracy in the assessment of 132 randomization integrity, accurate collection of specific endpoint procedures). These quality 133 factors are critical to the reliability and interpretability of the study data. 134
candidates.context: As noted above, in this guidance an important protocol deviation is a subset of protocol 118 deviations that might significantly affect the completeness, accuracy, and/or reliability of the 119 study data or that might significantly affect a subject’s rights, safety, or well-being. While other 120 terms such as major, critical, and significant have sometimes been used to classify such protocol 121 deviations, FDA recommends using important to encompass all these terms. 122 It may be helpful for a protocol to define important protocol deviations and provide examples of 136 what constitutes such for the particular study. candidates.statement: Investigators are responsible for protecting the rights, safety, and welfare of participants under 190 their care during a clinical investigation (21 CFR 312.60 and 812.100). Failing to comply with 191 aspects of the sponsor- and IRB-approved protocol that are designed to ensure that participants 192 are not exposed to unreasonable risks may be considered a failure to protect the rights, safety, 193 and welfare of participants. 13 When reporting protocol deviations to the sponsor, investigators 194 should identify important deviations. 195

candidates.statement: Sponsors are responsible for monitoring clinical investigations and ensuring the investigations 220 are conducted in accordance with the investigational plan and protocol (21 CFR 312.50, 812.40, 221 and 812.46). 15 Monitoring for protocol deviations during study conduct can help sponsors 222 identify site or study quality issues that can be addressed and improved; assessment of protocol 223 deviations after study completion can help in determining whether the study data are of sufficient 224 quality to be reliable and interpretable. Sponsors should also train investigators on the protocol 225 to facilitate their adherence to the protocol as well as provide training on identifying important 226 protocol deviations. candidates.statement: For protocol deviations not classified as important, sponsors should document and evaluate the 262 deviations to determine if the types and numbers of these protocol deviations warrant 263 reclassification; if the sponsor determines that reclassification is warranted, they should then 264 notify the investigator of the reclassification. Sponsors should carefully consider investigators’ 265 protocol deviation requests to determine whether a protocol amendment is needed to promote 266 consistent trial conduct by all investigators. Sponsors should incorporate appropriate degrees of 267 flexibility in the protocol so that intentional deviations will not be necessary. Irrespective of 268 sponsor approval of an intentional protocol deviation, investigators must get prior IRB approval 269 (21 CFR 312.66) unless there is an urgent need to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to 270 human subjects. 271

candidates.statement: When designing the study, sponsors should seek input from relevant stakeholders, including 295 potential trial participants and clinical investigators and their staff, to help ensure adherence to 296 the planned protocol by developing procedures that are feasible and not unnecessarily 297 burdensome. Before or during protocol development, sponsors should conduct a risk assessment 298 to identify protocol elements (e.g., visit structure, visit procedures, visit windows, enrollment 299 criteria) that can be made more flexible (or even eliminated entirely) to avoid the occurrence of 300 protocol deviations. Sponsors should also identify and document those protocol elements (e.g., 301 enrollment criteria, safety monitoring procedures, procedures related to primary or secondary 302 efficacy endpoints) that are critical to patient safety and data quality. 303

candidates.statement: Sponsors should assess the risks that such critical protocol elements may not be properly 305 conducted (e.g., complicated enrollment criteria, complex procedures), work to mitigate risks 306 associated with these elements, and then develop the study’s specific plans (e.g., medical 307 monitoring plan, safety monitoring plan, data management plan, risk-based monitoring plan, 308 independent endpoint adjudication charter) that will be used during the conduct of the trial to 309 further minimize the occurrence and the potential impact of important protocol deviations on 310 data quality or participants’ safety. 22 , 23 Further, investigators, site staff, study monitors, and 311 sponsor staff should be trained to focus on critical elements to ensure they are implemented as 312 specified in the protocol and associated study plans and to avoid important protocol deviations 313 that may impact trial participant safety or data quality. Finally, site monitors and centralized 314 monitoring activities should focus on critical elements for early identification of important 315 protocol deviations at specific sites or that suggest a pattern consistent with a systemic study 316 issue. 317

candidates.statement: Under applicable FDA regulations, the IRB is responsible for reviewing and approving the 333 initiation of and conducting periodic review of clinical investigations involving human subjects 334 (21 CFR 56.102(g)). The primary purpose of such review is to assure the protection of the rights 335 and welfare of human subjects (21 CFR 56.102(g)). IRBs must follow written procedures for 336 ensuring prompt reporting to the IRB of changes in research activity and for ensuring that 337 changes in approved research may not be initiated without IRB review and approval, except 338 where necessary to eliminate apparent immediate hazards to human subjects (21 CFR 339 56.108(a)(3) and (4)). 340

candidates.statement: Changes in a protocol are typically not implemented before review and approval by the IRB and, 360 in some cases, by FDA. Any modifications to protocol-specified procedures that occur without 361 prior IRB approval and submission to FDA of the protocol amendment implementing the 362 modification are considered protocol deviations. Sponsors and clinical investigators are 363 encouraged to engage with IRBs as early as possible when urgent or emergent changes to the 364 protocol or informed consent are anticipated. However, when changes to the protocol or 365 investigational plan are required to minimize or eliminate immediate hazards (e.g., rapidly 366 managing an evolving situation) or to protect the life and well-being of research participants, 367 they may be implemented without prior IRB approval or before filing an amendment to the IND 368 under 21 CFR 312.30(b)(2)(ii). A change to the protocol or investigational plan that is required 369 to minimize or eliminate immediate hazards is still considered a protocol deviation if it occurs 370 before IRB approval and should be reported as such (for additional information, see section 371 III.B). For devices, certain protocol changes or modifications to the investigational plan can be 372 made without prior FDA approval. 25 For example, a change or modification to the clinical 373 protocol may be reported in a 5-day notice if the changes do not affect (1) the validity of the data 374 or information resulting from the completion of the approved protocol or the relationship of 375 likely patient risk to benefit relied upon to approve the protocol; (2) the scientific soundness of 376
